MetaCheck Report

Clinical Prediction Model Performance Metrics Cluster at Arbitrary Thresholds and are Incorrectly Reported in High-Ranking Journals: An Observational Meta-Research Study

2026-11-22 · Metacheck 0.4.4.29 · DOI 10.64898/2026.11.02.26367135

3to fix2to check0to decide by hand0fine11not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 1656 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 1656 data columns across 286 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in 02_data/scimagojr_2024.csv. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: Publisher×2), so 2 of the file’s 27 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

  • Duplicated column names in alexdgibson/cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip/alexdgibson-cpm_auc-edfcfd2/02_data/scimagojr_2024.csv. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: Publisher×2), so 2 of the file’s 27 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

To fix Repository Check

What we found

  • We found 520 files in 3 repositories. The paper cites https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23875721 only in its reference list; we checked it as the authors’ deposit for this paper. Linking it in the data availability statement as well makes it easier to find.
  • We found 1 README file and 1 repository without READMEs.
  • We found 71 files with a naming suggestion.
  • We left out 2 files that do not belong in a repository: operating system (2). Remove them from the repository.
Show details

The paper cites https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23875721 only in its reference list; we checked it as the authors’ deposit for this paper. Linking it in the data availability statement as well makes it easier to find.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

The scripts load files, but 2 scripts loaded 2 files that could not be automatically identified in the repository. Check if the following files are made available, so that others can reproduce your code, or that the files are missing:

File name Missing Files
06_summary_stats.R example_data.csv
06_summary_stats.R example_data.csv

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 25 distinct packages/libraries: bayestestR, DescTools, DiagrammeR, dplyr, ggbrace, ggh4x, ggplot2, glue, irrCAC, janitor, jsonlite, lme4, mgcv, oddpub, openalexR, patchwork, plotROC, readxl, rentrez, roadoi, splines, stringr, tidyverse, tools, XML. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

The repository pins its analysis environment via a sessionInfo() record. Declared R version: 4.5.2.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 520 files: 292 data, 50 code, 4 documentation, 172 materials, 2 unknown.
  • We found 292 tabular data files and extracted 1656 columns from 286 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 3 study groups (ex1, ex2, pilot1), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 6 R workspace files (.RData/.rda) contain no reusable tabular data — only fitted models or saved session objects. Such files need R (and the exact packages used) to open and are not machine-readable. Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented .sav/.dta) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: 02_data/02_pilot/pilot_article.Rdata, 02_data/article.Rdata, 02_data/article_2.Rdata, alexdgibson/cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip/alexdgibson-cpm_auc-edfcfd2/02_data/02_pilot/pilot_article.Rdata, alexdgibson/cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip/alexdgibson-cpm_auc-edfcfd2/02_data/article.Rdata, alexdgibson/cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip/alexdgibson-cpm_auc-edfcfd2/02_data/article_2.Rdata. We ran automated data-quality checks on 1656 columns; 248 columns have at least one potential issue (134 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 42 columns with numeric values stored as text; 30 columns with inconsistent category casing; 24 columns whose values look like personal information; 20 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 10 columns whose name suggests personal information; 4 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 2 columns whose names become identical when special characters are removed; 2 columns with leading/trailing whitespace).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 1656 columns across 286 data files.

Issues Identified

248 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 286 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • 06_summary_stats.R reads example_data.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A package could not be installed.

  • 07_data_code_availability.R needs oddpub.
  • 08_data_code_availability.R needs oddpub.

oddpub is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/oddpub”) or BiocManager::install(“oddpub”), with the version you used.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • 10_analysis_adrian.R: plot_data

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • 02_article_extraction.R
  • 02_article_extraction_2.R
  • 03_pilot_articles.R
  • 05_predict_research_time.R

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • 02_extract_auc_roc.R
  • 11_roc_analysis.R

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • 02_article_extraction.R reads files under another name than the deposit holds (q_one_journals.rdata -> q_one_journals.Rdata). We corrected the names so the script could run; they should be changed in the script.
  • 02_article_extraction_2.R reads files under another name than the deposit holds (q_one_journals.rdata -> q_one_journals.Rdata). We corrected the names so the script could run; they should be changed in the script.
  • 03_pilot_articles.R reads files under another name than the deposit holds (journal_rank.rdata -> journal_rank.Rdata). We corrected the names so the script could run; they should be changed in the script.

File paths

3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: 02_data/journal_rank.rdata to 02_data/journal_rank.Rdata (in 03_pilot_articles.R); 02_data/q_one_journals.rdata to 02_data/q_one_journals.Rdata (in 02_article_extraction.R); 02_data/q_one_journals.rdata to 02_data/q_one_journals.Rdata (in 02_article_extraction_2.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside alexdgibson/cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("cpm_auc-pre_print_release.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked.

3 file names in the code are not the same as in the deposit, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

File Name in the code Name in the deposit

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 24 scripts: 14 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 4 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: 02_article_extraction.R, 02_article_extraction_2.R, 03_pilot_articles.R, 05_predict_research_time.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. 1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: 10_plots_for_slides.R after 10_analysis.R. Such a script should source() the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

a script hit an object '...' not found error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first; a script hit a could not find function "..." error; we added the library() calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
10_analysis_adrian.R plot_data (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

Dependency-unavailable errors

2 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

File
07_data_code_availability.R
08_data_code_availability.R

library() calls added

1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

> sens_hand_more <- sens_agreement_df %>% filter(hand == "present" & claude == "missing") %>% filter(!is.na(sens))
> sens_claude_more <- sens_agreement_df %>% filter(claude == "present" & hand == "missing") %>% filter(!is.na(sens))
> set.seed(42)
> hand_sample_sens <- slice_sample(sens_hand_more, n = 50)
> claude_sample_sens <- slice_sample(sens_claude_more, n = 50)
> sens_extra <- rbind(hand_sample_sens,
>                    claude_sample_sens) %>% 
>   select(doi, sens, claude, hand, agreement)
> claude_flag_spec <- claude_sub %>%
>   group_by(doi, spec) %>%
>   mutate(occ = row_number()) %>% 
>   ungroup()
> hand_flag_spec <- hand_sub %>%
>   group_by(doi, spec) %>%
>   mutate(occ = row_number()) %>% 
>   ungroup()
> spec_agreement_df <- full_join(
>   claude_flag_spec %>% select(doi, spec, occ) %>% mutate(claude = "present"),
>   hand_flag_spec   %>% select(doi, spec, occ) %>% mutate(hand   = "present"),
>   by = c("doi", "spec", "occ")
> ) %>%
>   mutate(
>     claude = ifelse(is.na(claude), "missing", claude),
>     hand   = ifelse(is.na(hand),   "missing", hand),
>     agreement = case_when(
>       claude == "present" & hand == "present" ~ "both",
>       claude == "present"                     ~ "claude_only",
>       hand   == "present"                     ~ "hand_only",
>       hand   == "missing" & claude == "missing" ~ "both"
>     )
>   )

> spec_hand_more <- spec_agreement_df %>% filter(hand == "present" & claude == "missing") %>% filter(!is.na(spec))
> spec_claude_more <- spec_agreement_df %>% filter(claude == "present" & hand == "missing") %>% filter(!is.na(spec))
> set.seed(42)
> hand_sample_spec <- slice_sample(spec_hand_more, n = 50)
> claude_sample_spec <- slice_sample(spec_claude_more, n = 50)
> spec_extra <- rbind(hand_sample_spec,
>                     claude_sample_spec) %>% 
>   select(doi, spec, claude, hand, agreement)
> claude_flag_sample_size <- claude_sub %>%
>   group_by(doi, sample_size) %>%
>   mutate(occ = row_number()) %>% 
>   ungroup()
> hand_flag_sample_size <- hand_sub %>%
>   group_by(doi, sample_size) %>%
>   mutate(occ = row_number()) %>% 
>   ungroup()
> sample_size_agreement_df <- full_join(
>   claude_flag_sample_size %>% select(doi, sample_size, occ) %>% mutate(claude = "present"),
>   hand_flag_sample_size   %>% select(doi, sample_size, occ) %>% mutate(hand   = "present"),
>   by = c("doi", "sample_size", "occ")
> ) %>%
>   mutate(
>     claude = ifelse(is.na(claude), "missing", claude),
>     hand   = ifelse(is.na(hand),   "missing", hand),
>     agreement = case_when(
>       claude == "present" & hand == "present" ~ "both",
>       claude == "present"                     ~ "claude_only",
>       hand   == "present"                     ~ "hand_only",
>       hand   == "missing" & claude == "missing" ~ "both"
>     )
>   )

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

An ethics approval statement was detected, based on the following text:

This study didn’t require ethics approval as it used publicly available data and there are no risks to data collection.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
